verdict.rationale: The word-level pattern is dense, recurring, and convergent across the New Testament. Three distinct residence verbs are used of the Spirit in believers: 'dwells' (oikeo) in the present indicative (an ongoing, simple statement of fact), as in 'the Spirit of God dwells in you', Romans 8:9, 1 Corinthians 3:16; the intensified compound 'in-dwells' (enoikeo), as in 'the Spirit indwelling us', Romans 8:11, 2 Timothy 1:14; and 'stays' (meno), as in 'the Spirit of truth stays alongside you', John 14:17. Each of these verbs carries the locative phrase 'in you' (en hymin) or 'in us' (en hemin). The 'temple' image (naos) at 1 Corinthians 3:16, 6:19, and 2 Corinthians 6:16, plus the pledge terms 'downpayment' (arrabon) and 'sealed' (sphragizo) at Ephesians 1:13-14, add a second and third independent line of evidence. The negative test in Romans 8:9, 'if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this one is not his' (ei tis pneuma Christou ouk echei, houtos ouk estin autou), makes possession of the indwelling Spirit coextensive with belonging to Christ, leaving no class of true believer without the Spirit. Permanence is encoded by 'into the age' (eis ton aiona) in John 14:16 and 'downpayment' (arrabon) in Ephesians 1:14. The same dwelling verb 'dwells' (oikeo) also takes sin as its subject in Romans 7:17-20, which shows the verb is location-neutral (it names residence without naming the resident) and the doctrine rides on the subject of the sentence, the Spirit, not on the verb alone. But every occurrence with the Spirit as subject points in one direction.

scripture.force: Twin 'if-then' contrast (conditional). 'You are not in flesh but in Spirit, since the Spirit of God dwells in you' uses 'dwells' (oikei, present indicative of oikeo, an ongoing, simple statement of fact) with the locative phrase 'in you' (en hymin), asserting an ongoing residence. The follow-up clause, 'if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, this one is not his' (ei tis pneuma Christou ouk echei, houtos ouk estin autou), makes 'have' (echo) of the Spirit a definitional test for belonging to Christ, ruling out a true believer who lacks the indwelling. Token check confirms 'dwells' (oikeo), 'in' (en), 'have' (echo), the negation 'not' (ou), and the indefinite 'anyone' (tis) are all present in Romans 8:9.

The 'if-then' clause (conditional), 'if Christ is in you' (ei de Christos en hymin), parallels the prior Spirit clause and extends the indwelling to Christ by the Spirit. 'The body is reckoned dead because of sin but the spirit is life because of righteousness' indicates a present saving reality, not a future or intermittent state.

The participle 'in-dwelling' (enoikoun, present of enoikeo, the intensified compound meaning 'to in-dwell') is applied to the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus, dwelling 'in you' (en hymin). The compound form (en 'in' plus oikeo 'dwell') makes the locative force explicit, and the present tense marks habitual residence. The same indwelling Spirit is also the guarantee of bodily resurrection, tying indwelling to end-time completion.

'Do you not know that you are God's temple and the Spirit of God dwells in you' ('the Spirit of God dwells in you', to pneuma tou theou oikei en hymin)? Token check confirms 'dwells' (oikeo), 'temple' (naos), 'in' (en), and 'God' (theos) together in one clause. This pairs the same dwelling verb as Romans 8:9 with the temple image, addressed to the whole congregation, which extends the indwelling claim from individuals to the collective body of believers and uses the present tense for ongoing residence.

Jesus promises to ask the Father, who will give 'another Helper' or 'another Advocate' (allon parakleton, 'another' of the same kind) to be with the disciples 'into the age' (eis ton aiona). The temporal phrase 'into the age' (eis ton aiona) marks unending duration in Johannine usage and grammatically attaches to the giving, not to any conditional retention. This is the explicit permanence anchor.

The 'Helper' or 'Advocate' (Paraclete) is 'the Spirit of truth' (to pneuma tes aletheias). Two prepositional clauses describe location, 'stays alongside you' (par hymin menei) and 'will be in you' (en hymin estai). Token check confirms 'stays' (meno), the preposition 'alongside' (para), 'in' (en), and the future of 'to be' (eimi). The verb 'stays' (meno) plus the future 'will be' (estai) specify continued and incoming residence, distinguishing the disciples from the world that cannot receive him. The clause boundary between 'stays' (menei) and 'will be' (estai) marks a transition from alongside to within, not a withdrawal.

Rhetorical question: 'do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you' (tou en hymin hagiou pneumatos), 'whom you have from God' (hou echete apo theou)? Token check confirms 'temple' (naos), 'body' (soma), 'in' (en), and 'have' (echo). The 'temple' (naos) image presupposes ongoing residence, and 'you have' (echete, present indicative of echo, an ongoing, simple statement of fact) again predicates possession of the Spirit on the believer.

'For we are the temple of the living God, as God said, I will dwell in them and walk among them' ('I will in-dwell in them', enoikeso en autois). Token check confirms 'in-dwell' (enoikeo), 'temple' (naos), 'God' (theos), 'in' (en), and the walking verb 'walk among' (emperipateo). The first-person future 'I will in-dwell' (enoikeso) has God himself as the explicit subject of the indwelling, picking up an Old Testament dwelling promise and applying it to the believing community, which grounds the New Testament indwelling in the divine self-commitment to dwell among his people.

'Guard the good deposit through the Holy Spirit who indwells in us' ('through the Holy Spirit, the one in-dwelling in us', dia pneumatos hagiou tou enoikountos en hemin). Token check confirms 'in-dwell' (enoikeo), 'in' (en), and the preposition 'through' (dia). The participle 'in-dwelling' (enoikountos), the same compound as in Romans 8:11, with the first-person plural 'in us' (en hemin), broadens the indwelling beyond the Roman and Corinthian audiences to a general first-person plural, supporting the every-believer scope.

Sequence: 'having heard, having believed, you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise' ('you were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise', esphragisthete to pneumati tes epangelias to hagio). Token check confirms 'seal' (sphragizo), the participles of 'hear' (akouo) and 'believe' (pisteuo), and 'promise' (epangelia). The aorist passive 'you were sealed' (esphragisthete, a completed past action done to the believer) with the participial chain places the sealing at the point of faith, not as a later stage. Sealing as an image for ownership and security supports both initiation and permanence of the indwelling.

The Spirit is the 'downpayment' or 'earnest' (arrabon, a commercial term for a deposit guaranteeing the rest of a transaction) of our inheritance, 'unto the redemption of the possession' (eis apolytrosin tes peripoieseos). Token check confirms 'downpayment' (arrabon), 'redemption' (apolytrosis), and 'inheritance' (kleronomia). The 'downpayment' (arrabon) image guarantees the rest of the transaction, so the Spirit's present indwelling is the legal pledge of future glorification, which secures permanence on the indwelling itself. The same 'downpayment' (arrabon) term recurs at 2 Corinthians 1:22 and 2 Corinthians 5:5, all of the Spirit.

'It is no longer I who do it but sin that dwells in me' ('the dwelling-in-me sin', he oikousa en emoi hamartia). Token grounding shows the same verb 'dwells' (oikeo) with the same locative phrase 'in me' (en emoi) but with sin, not the Spirit, as its subject, repeated at Romans 7:17 and 7:18. This demonstrates that 'dwells' (oikeo) by itself is location-neutral (it names residence without naming the resident) and does not name what dwells. The indwelling doctrine therefore rests on the identity of the subject in the indwelling clauses, the Spirit of God, not on the bare verb, which is why this verse complicates a naive verb-only argument without weakening the verdict.

complicating_texts.resolution: The dwelling verb 'dwells' (oikeo) at Romans 7:17, 7:18, and 7:20 takes sin ('sin', hamartia) as its subject, dwelling 'in me' (en emoi), not the Spirit. Queried distribution confirms 'dwells' (oikeo) occurs nine times in the canon and the subject varies (sin in Romans 7, the Spirit in Romans 8:9 and 1 Corinthians 3:16, a believing or unbelieving spouse in 1 Corinthians 7:12-13, God in unapproachable light in 1 Timothy 6:16). This proves the verb is location-neutral (it names residence without naming the resident) and does not by itself name the indweller. The indwelling-of-the-Spirit verdict therefore rests on the subject of the clause in Romans 8 and 1 Corinthians 3, where the subject is explicitly the Spirit of God, not on the bare verb. The verdict is unaffected once the subject is fixed.

The Davidic plea, 'do not take your Holy Spirit from me', belongs to an earlier covenantal pattern where the Spirit empowered specific roles (king, prophet, craftsman) and could be withdrawn (compare 1 Samuel 16:14). The Johannine and Pauline indwelling texts mark a later, settled gift, with John 14:16 promising the 'Helper' or 'Advocate' (Paraclete) 'into the age' (eis ton aiona) and the canon itself cross-linking John 14:17 to Ezekiel 36:27 (38 OpenBible votes), the promise to put the Spirit within. The word-level permanence in the New Testament verses is not contradicted by the earlier withdrawal language because the arrangement described differs. The Hebrew Spirit-withdrawal vocabulary is not queryable at lemma depth in this store, so this resolution rests on the New Testament permanence terms and the cross-ref bridge, not on a counted Hebrew anchor.

The exhortation, 'do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption', is the cross-referenced link from Ephesians 1:13-14. Token data confirms 'seal' (sphragizo, G4972) at both Ephesians 1:13 and Ephesians 4:30. The verse warns against grieving but presupposes continued indwelling and sealing 'for the day of redemption' (eis hemeran apolytroseos). At the word level, it reinforces permanence rather than threatening it.

The verse distinguishes the world (which cannot receive the Spirit) from disciples (with whom he stays and in whom he will be). The clause boundary between 'stays' (menei, present) and 'will be' (estai, future of 'to be', eimi) has been read by some as a future-only indwelling, but 'stays' (meno) occurs 119 times in the canon, heavily in Johannine abiding language (John 15:4-7, 1 John 2:24, 3:24, 4:13) for stable ongoing residence, and the future 'will be' (estai) marks the Pentecost transition from alongside to within rather than a conditional or temporary state. The continuous-indwelling reading is the dominant one at the word level.

variant_units_examined.note: Witnesses vary between accusative (the direct-object grammatical form, dia to enoikoun autou pneuma) and genitive (the 'of-X' grammatical form, dia tou enoikountos autou pneumatos) constructions for the agency of resurrection. Both readings retain 'in-dwell' (enoikeo) applied to the Spirit in believers, so the indwelling claim is invariant across the variant. This verse is outside the ingested ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) 3 John window, so the apparatus reading is recorded from morphology, not from CBGM (Coherence-Based Genealogical Method) data.

Wider ECM (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) for the Pauline and Johannine corpora is not yet published in this store, so status is recorded as ecm-shadow rather than ecm-published.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Three dwelling verbs, 'dwells' (oikeo), 'in-dwells' (enoikeo), and 'stays' (meno), with the locative phrases 'in you' (en hymin) and 'in us' (en hemin), spread across the gospel and four Pauline letters; the 'temple' (naos) image at 1 Corinthians 3:16, 6:19, and 2 Corinthians 6:16; and the pledge terms 'downpayment' (arrabon) and 'sealed' (sphragizo) at Ephesians 1:13-14 converge on a present residence that begins at faith and is guaranteed for the future. The negative test at Romans 8:9 makes having the Spirit definitional of belonging to Christ, so no true believer is excluded.

Earlier Spirit-coming and Spirit-withdrawal language (Judges 16:20, 1 Samuel 16:14, Psalm 51:11) describes the Spirit empowering particular persons for particular tasks, with possible withdrawal. Stated at its strongest, this lens reads the indwelling texts as the culmination of a promise (the canon itself links John 14:17 to Ezekiel 36:27) rather than a flat denial of any change. The New Testament terms 'into the age' (eis ton aiona) and 'downpayment' (arrabon) supply the duration that the earlier pattern lacked, so the lens informs the timeline without overturning the verdict.

Stated fairly, this lens reads the sealing of Ephesians 1:13 or the receiving of the Spirit as a stage after initial faith. The grammar resists it. The participles 'having heard' (akousantes) and 'having believed' (pisteusantes) together with the aorist passive 'you were sealed' (esphragisthete, a completed past action done to the believer) in Ephesians 1:13 align hearing, believing, and sealing as one event, and Romans 8:9 makes 'have' (echo) of the Spirit the test of belonging to Christ, which a class of Spirit-less true believers would falsify. The verb tenses, not church practice, are what decide against the second-stage reading here.

A reading that argues the doctrine from the dwelling verb alone is incomplete, because 'dwells' (oikeo) at Romans 7:17-20 takes sin as its subject in the same locative construction. The verb names residence, not the resident. The strongest form of the doctrine specifies the subject of each clause (the Spirit of God, Christ, God himself) rather than leaning on the verb, and on that basis the verdict holds.

hermeneutics.notes: Progressive revelation (the idea that God reveals himself in stages across the canon) is in play because the duration terms 'into the age' (eis ton aiona) and 'downpayment' (arrabon) attach to the later indwelling texts and the canon cross-links the promise to Ezekiel 36:27. The 'analogy of Scripture' (analogia scripturae, the practice of letting clearer passages clarify less clear ones) harmonizes the earlier withdrawal texts with the later permanence terms by fixing the subject and the covenantal timeline, both from the words themselves.

stem_audit.notes: The stem uses 'true believer', which is descriptive rather than tradition-loaded, and the words 'permanently' and 'from the moment of regeneration' are the testable word-level claims, carried by 'in-dwell' (enoikeo) and 'into the age' (eis ton aiona) for permanence, by 'you were sealed' (esphragisthete) aligned with the believing participles for the moment of faith, and by the Romans 8:9 'have' (echo) test for every-believer scope. The verb-only objection (that 'dwells' (oikeo) also dwells of sin in Romans 7) was examined and resolved by fixing the clause subject. Verdict affirms unchanged from the prior file; lexical work widened the spread to gospel plus epistle, so pan_canonical (spread across the whole Bible) was raised from false to true.

lay_summary: The Greek New Testament uses three different dwelling words for the Holy Spirit and the believer. In Romans 8:9-11 Paul uses 'dwells' (oikeo) and the stronger compound 'in-dwells' (enoikeo), both in the present tense, locating the Spirit inside the believer with the phrase 'in you' (en hymin). The same 'in-dwells' (enoikeo) recurs at 2 Timothy 1:14, 'the Spirit who indwells in us', and at 2 Corinthians 6:16, where God himself says 'I will dwell in them'. In John 14:16-17 Jesus uses 'stays' (meno), 'stays alongside', and the future 'will be in you', with the explicit phrase 'into the age' (eis ton aiona) marking permanence. In 1 Corinthians 3:16 and 6:19 Paul calls believers a 'temple' (naos) of the Spirit who is in you and whom you have from God. In Ephesians 1:13-14 believers were sealed at the point of believing, and the Spirit is the 'downpayment' (arrabon, a commercial pledge), guaranteeing the inheritance. Across these texts the pattern is consistent. The Spirit resides in the believer, the residence begins at faith, and it is tied to permanence. Romans 8:9 adds a sharp negative test. The one who does not have the Spirit of Christ is not Christ's, which makes having the indwelling Spirit definitional of being a true believer. One honest wrinkle in the words. The verb 'dwells' (oikeo) is location-neutral (it names residence without naming the resident). In Romans 7:17-20 the very same verb has sin, not the Spirit, as what dwells in a person. So the doctrine does not ride on the verb alone but on the subject of each sentence, and in every indwelling clause that subject is named as the Spirit of God, Christ, or God. Read that way, the spread across a gospel and several letters all points one direction, and the text supports both halves of the claim. The Spirit indwells every true believer, and that indwelling is permanent.
